title: The effect of Relativistic Aberration on Cosmological Distances

predicted_errors.error_location: Eq. (3) and surrounding justification for an expansion-induced relative velocity
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The derivation treats coordinates as a covector: it writes x_i=g_ik x^k and hence v_i=d(g_ik x^k)/dτ. Coordinates x^i are not components of a vector field and cannot generally be lowered with the metric. The covariant four-velocity is u_i=g_ik dx^k/dτ, not d(g_ik x^k)/dτ. Thus the claimed metric-derivative contribution to a galaxy's velocity, on which the later argument relies, is invalid.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, from the assertion that FLRW redshift is 'only the relativistic Doppler effect' through Eqs. (4)-(5)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper assigns every cosmological source a single special-relativistic relative speed β=[(1+z)^2-1]/[(1+z)^2+1] and treats source and observer as globally related inertial frames. In FLRW spacetime, distant comoving worldlines do not possess a unique, path-independent relative velocity; cosmological redshift is determined by the scale-factor ratio (or accumulated local shifts along the null geodesic), not by one Lorentz transformation between distant local frames. Local inertial frames do not justify applying a single SR aberration transformation across cosmological separation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Immediately after Eq. (5): 'if the expansion ... between us and the CO is faster than c, ... we simply can't detect any light signal'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This is false in FLRW cosmology. Superluminal recession velocity is coordinate-dependent and does not define an event horizon. We routinely receive light from objects that were receding faster than c when they emitted it, including the CMB; whether light reaches us depends on the null geodesic and expansion history, not on whether a recession speed exceeds c at one epoch.

predicted_errors.error_location: Eqs. (6), (11)-(18), especially the claimed extra (1+z)^-2 photon fraction and flux factor
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The asserted aberration correction double-counts the optical geometry already present in the FLRW distance calculation. Eq. (6), b≈R(t0)r1 ε, is the source-side solid-angle/area mapping obtained from the null-geodesic bundle. Applying a further SR transformation to that same aperture angle and then declaring that an isotropic source emits fewer photons into it produces the spurious extra (1+z)^-2 in Eqs. (13)-(15). In metric cosmology with photon-number conservation the standard result is F=L/[4πD_M^2(1+z)^2], where D_M=R0 r1 (for the displayed radial coordinate), not the paper's additional (1+z)^-2 suppression.

predicted_errors.error_location: Eqs. (16), (24), (29), (39), and (40): revised luminosity and angular distances
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proposed distances are one factor of (1+z) away from the standard geometrical distances. With D_M=R0r1, FLRW gives d_A=D_M/(1+z)=R(t1)r1 and d_L=(1+z)D_M=(1+z)^2d_A. The paper instead gives d_L=R0^3/R1^2 r1=(1+z)^2D_M and Eq. (40) gives d_A=D_M. Although their ratio is arranged to retain d_L=(1+z)^2d_A, both individual definitions no longer equal the operational area/flux distances. Etherington reciprocity is not evidence for the altered definitions; it is precisely the theorem that, with the operational definitions, yields the standard expressions.

predicted_errors.error_location: Eqs. (19)-(20) and the claimed alternative derivation of Eq. (18)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The statement that dV_p=ν dΩ dν is an invariant integration element on the light cone is not a correct invariant phase-space measure. Momentum-space volume contains ν^2dνdΩ (and invariant measures include appropriate energy and spacetime factors); νdΩdν alone is neither dimensionally nor Lorentz invariant as asserted. Therefore it cannot establish the angular transformation or the extra beaming factor.

The cosmological-time/redshift relation has the wrong sign: along the past light cone dt/dz=-1/[(1+z)H(z)], whereas Eq. (34) gives a positive value. Further, Eq. (34) uses (1+z)^2(1+Ω_M z)-z(2+z)Ω_Λ, while Eq. (36) defines H with (1+z^2)(1+Ω_Mz)-zΩ_Λ(2+z); these are not the same expression. This changes the expansion function and makes the subsequent integration internally inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Eqs. (35)-(37), and use of r1 in Eqs. (39), (46), and (47)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Eq. (35) states R0 f(r1)=H0^-1∫dz/E, but Eq. (37) sets r1=F(√|Ωk|∫dz/E), omitting the required scale factors and 1/√|Ωk| (and, depending on units, c/(R0H0)). It therefore does not solve Eq. (35). The later equations inconsistently insert c/(H0√|Ωk|) outside r1. Moreover Eq. (46) explicitly uses r1(z,0,...) while Eq. (37), read literally, gives zero for Ωk=0; the required flat-curvature limit is neither written nor consistently defined.

The claimed CMB solid-angle stretching by about 10^6 is obtained by treating z_CMB≈1000 as an observer/source SR boost. That is not the physical CMB aberration effect. Observable CMB aberration is generated by the observer's peculiar velocity relative to the CMB (β≈1.2×10^-3), producing small direction remapping and multipole coupling. Cosmological redshift from last scattering is not a coherent Lorentz boost that spreads every CMB patch by (1+z)^2. The conclusions that the CMB's isotropy may be an aberrational mixing artifact and that CMB parameter inference requires this correction consequently have no valid derivation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1-3.2 claims that supernova cosmological parameters, curvature, and dark energy may be wrong because of the proposed correction
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: These conclusions depend entirely on the invalid extra flux factor and non-operational distances. Standard SN analyses already use the FLRW luminosity distance, which incorporates redshift, time dilation, and null-bundle geometry. No data reanalysis, likelihood calculation, fit, uncertainty propagation, or observational residual test is provided. The paper therefore cannot support claims that Ω_M, Ω_Λ, curvature, or acceleration have been systematically mismeasured.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.3 statement that the age 'vary very little' with cosmological parameters and 'depends strongly only on H0'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: At fixed H0 the cosmic age is H0^-1 times an expansion-history integral and can vary substantially with Ω_M, Ω_Λ, and curvature. For example, an Einstein-de Sitter model has t0=2/(3H0), unlike the approximately 0.96/H0 age of standard flat ΛCDM. Thus this assertion is not a valid reason to dismiss the consequences of changing density parameters.

The proposed neutron-star-mass test is physically misstated. Compact-binary masses are primarily inferred from the gravitational-wave phase evolution, while amplitude determines a luminosity-distance/inclination combination; they are not obtained simply by a Fourier transform of an observed 'flux.' Also, 'Volkov-Oppenheimer limit' is not the relevant named limit; the standard neutron-star stability bound is the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit. The suggested test does not follow from the derivation.

The paper cites a large number of works throughout (e.g., Einstein 1905/1916, Ellis et al. 2012, Carroll et al. 1992, Perlmutter et al. 1999, Planck Collaboration et al. 2016, Thorne 1981, and many others), but the supplied bibliography contains only Weinberg (1972) and Bunn & Hogg (2009), plus the stray text “3C 279 on page 1.” This prevents verification of the claimed sources and does not meet the basic citation requirement for the many attributed formulas and factual assertions.
